topic.title: Sanctuary cities
topic.proposition: Cities should limit their local police's cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: I understand the humanitarian impulse behind sanctuary policies, but I think local police cooperating with federal immigration enforcement is just basic rule of law. When cities limit that cooperation, they're effectively picking and choosing which federal laws matter, and that undermines trust in the whole system. Public safety should come from everyone playing by the same rules, not from carving out exceptions based on a person's immigration status. I worry this sends a signal that some laws are optional.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: I hear the rule-of-law concern, but in my view the more pressing issue is that when local police act as an arm of federal immigration enforcement, immigrant communities stop reporting crimes or cooperating with investigations at all. That makes everyone less safe, not more, because victims and witnesses go silent out of fear. Local police exist to handle local public safety, and conflating that mission with federal civil enforcement blurs a line that protects trust between officers and the communities they serve. I think that trust is worth protecting even if it means stepping back from certain federal requests.

messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: That's a fair point about trust, and I don't dismiss the fear some communities feel. But I think there's a difference between handling civil immigration matters and refusing to hand over someone who's already been arrested for a separate crime. When local police decline those handoffs, it can let genuinely dangerous individuals back onto the street before federal agents can act, and that puts the whole community at risk, not just the person involved. I think public safety requires some baseline cooperation, especially when someone has already been through the local justice system.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: I understand that worry, and I agree public safety matters enormously here, but civil detainer requests aren't the same as a judicial warrant, and holding someone past their release date on a civil request alone raises real legal and constitutional concerns for cities. I think that distinction is exactly why policies should draw a line at voluntary civil cooperation rather than treating every federal request as automatically binding. This is the claim I am relying on. Connecticut bars police and jail staff from honoring civil immigration holds unless the individual is on a terror watch list or has been convicted of a severe violent felony
